passage: In the small-town school, Class 10, Manjula's group of four had to finish a file on soil types for Monday. The other three had promised sections. By Sunday afternoon Manjula had written all of them, redrawn two maps and stapled the pages. Pradeep, the group leader, had sent only a text: "you are so good at this, thanks!" Manjula wanted to say it was not fair, but she thought of being called bossy, like last time, and typed, "Fine, no problem." She pressed the staples down so hard the paper tore. Then she put the torn corner in her bag and told nobody.

qa.q: What did Pradeep send to Manjula on Sunday?
qa.a: Pradeep sent a text: "you are so good at this, thanks!"

qa.q: Why did Manjula type "Fine, no problem" although she wanted to say it was not fair?
qa.a: Manjula feared being called bossy, so the anger stayed hidden and built quietly; the torn paper shows the strength of that unspoken resentment.

qa.q: What could Manjula say to the group before the next deadline?
qa.a: Manjula could name the sections she finished and ask each person to send theirs by a set time, framed as sharing the work rather than blaming anyone.

qa.q: What might Pradeep be thinking when sending only a text of thanks?
qa.a: Pradeep may believe the praise is enough, or not realise how heavy the work was; the cheerful text suggests not seeing Manjula's resentment.

grounding: A conscientious student ends up doing most of a shared task and grows resentful, fearing that complaining will look bossy.

passage: In a Vancouver Grade 10 class, Kwame stayed until six on Thursday finishing the group science presentation. Xin had promised the graphs and Ines the conclusion; both arrived on Friday with nothing but jokes. Kwame's jaw tightened. "We can share the rest at lunch?" Ines suggested brightly. "Sure," said Kwame. Inside, Kwame was seething. During the presentation Xin got the biggest smile from the teacher. Kwame said nothing then either, only smiled thinly, and wrote in a private notebook, "Next time I will say it early. But saying it feels bossy."

qa.q: Until what time did Kwame stay on Thursday?
qa.a: Kwame stayed until six on Thursday finishing the group science presentation.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling when saying "Sure" to Ines?
qa.a: Kwame was seething with anger inside while sounding polite; the tight jaw shows resentment being swallowed to avoid looking bossy.

qa.q: What could Kwame do at the start of the next group project?
qa.a: Kwame could suggest early who does what and when, and check in midweek, so the imbalance is visible before it becomes resentment.

qa.q: How might Ines have seen Friday's lunch offer?
qa.a: Ines probably saw it as a friendly solution and may not have noticed how much work Kwame had done; the bright tone suggests no awareness of the anger.

grounding: A conscientious student ends up doing most of a shared task and grows resentful, fearing that complaining will look bossy.

passage:
Hey Pradeep bhaiya,
Can I vent for a minute? The civics project is due Monday. There are four of us. I have done the survey, the graphs AND the report. Tanmay made one chart. Riya and Sameer said they'd “check it over”.
Every time I think about messaging the group, I imagine them saying, “Chill, Vishal, why are you so bossy?” So I don't. I just do more.
Last night at 1 am I was fixing Sameer's paragraph and I actually slammed my laptop shut. I'm so angry I can't concentrate in class.
How did you deal with this in college? I don't want to be the villain, but I'm so tired of being the servant.
Vishal

qa.q: What has Vishal done for the project?
qa.a: Vishal has done the survey, the graphs and the report.

qa.q: Why doesn't Vishal message the group?
qa.a: Vishal is afraid of seeming bossy, so the anger stays quiet and keeps building.

qa.q: What would you advise Vishal to do before Monday?
qa.a: Vishal could send a calm message listing the tasks left with a name and time next to each, which is organising, not bossing.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see the situation?
qa.a: Pradeep will probably see that Vishal is overloaded and resentful, and may encourage clear, calm words with the group.

grounding: A teenager writes about doing most of a group task alone, growing angry but afraid that complaining will seem bossy.

passage:
So the podcast theme is group projects? Okay. I'm Varun, and I'll be honest. I hated them.
In Class 9 our group had to make a documentary about our neighbourhood. Yamini said she'd do the interviews. She didn't. Aman said he'd edit. He didn't. So I did the interviews, the filming, the editing, three nights till one.
I never said anything. I was scared they'd call me bossy, the one who ruins the mood. Instead I just went quieter and quieter. I'd answer them in one word.
At the screening, everyone clapped for our team. Yamini hugged me. I smiled and wanted to scream.
Now I know: it wasn't them I was angry at most. It was me, for never saying a word.

qa.q: How many nights did Varun work till one?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when Yamini hugged him at the screening?
qa.a: Varun felt angry and resentful, smiling on the outside while wanting to scream inside.

qa.q: What could Varun have said early on without sounding bossy?
qa.a: Varun could have calmly reminded the group of the tasks each had agreed to, with a clear date, before doing everything alone.

qa.q: How might Yamini have seen the project?
qa.a: Yamini may have thought everything was fine, since Varun said nothing, and hugged him without seeing the resentment.

grounding: A teenager recalls carrying a group documentary alone, too afraid of seeming bossy to complain, so anger built quietly.

passage:
Monday: The science exhibition group split the work. Abhinav wrote the plan. Bidisha said she'd do the model. Karan said he'd do the poster.
Thursday: No model. No poster. Abhinav stayed after school and started both. When Bidisha passed by, he smiled and said, “No problem, I've got it.” He didn't mean it. He just didn't want to look like the bossy one.
The next Tuesday: The night before the exhibition, Abhinav was gluing the model at eleven while group messages about a cricket match pinged on his phone. He snapped a pencil in half. At the exhibition Bidisha explained the model to the judges. Abhinav stood beside her with his jaw tight, saying nothing.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say she'd do?
qa.a: Bidisha said she'd do the model.

qa.q: What does Abhinav snapping the pencil suggest?
qa.a: It suggests his anger and resentment were building up because he felt he couldn't complain without seeming bossy.

qa.q: What small step could Abhinav have taken on Thursday?
qa.a: He could have told Bidisha and Karan kindly but clearly that he needed their parts by Saturday, instead of saying "No problem".

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel if she knew what Abhinav went through?
qa.a: She might feel embarrassed and sorry, realising he did her part while she took the credit.

grounding: Shows a conscientious student quietly doing most of a group project, growing resentful but fearing he'll look bossy if he complains.

passage:
Lakshmi, you say your group leaves the whole science model to you? Sit. Let your Abhinav thatha tell you something.
Class 9, Madurai, long ago. Our teacher put four of us on a river-system chart: Ravi, Selvam, Mani and me. Within a week, I was the only one drawing. Ravi said his handwriting was bad. Selvam had cricket. Mani just smiled.
I didn't complain. I thought they'd call me bossy, the one who thinks he's the teacher. So I sat up by the kerosene lamp, grinding my teeth, and the anger sat in me like a stone. The night before submission, I tore a whole page because one line was crooked.
My amma saw and asked what was wrong, and I told her everything. Next morning I told Selvam plainly, "You colour the mountains, or your name comes off the chart."
He coloured them. Badly. But he did it.

qa.q: What reason did Ravi give for not drawing?
qa.a: Ravi said his handwriting was bad.

qa.q: How did young Abhinav feel while doing the chart alone?
qa.a: He felt angry and resentful, the anger sitting "like a stone", but afraid that complaining would make the others call him bossy.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Telling his amma and then speaking plainly to Selvam; saying it aloud let the anger out and made the work shared.

qa.q: How might Selvam have felt when Abhinav spoke so plainly?
qa.a: Selvam was probably surprised and a little embarrassed that the quiet one had noticed, which is why he did his part.

grounding: Shows a conscientious student doing most of a shared task alone, growing quietly resentful because complaining might look bossy.
